hook.en: You want a recycling unit in your school, or a reading corner in the library. A proposal sets out the plan so clearly that the reader can say yes.

objectives.en: Recognise the headings of an ISC-style proposal
Write each section in clear, impersonal language
Turn given notes into a complete, well-organised proposal

narration.en: You want a recycling unit in your school, or a reading corner in the library. A proposal sets out the plan so clearly that the reader can say yes.

body.en: A proposal is a formal plan for an activity, project or change, written for those who must approve it. It is usually organised under headings: a title; an introduction or background (the situation and why action is needed); objectives or aims; the plan of action or method (steps, people, schedule); resources or budget needed; expected benefits or outcomes; and a conclusion. The language is clear, formal and impersonal (It is proposed that …), and points under each heading may be listed briefly.

title.en: On the board: a proposal, section by section

say.en: A proposal moves from the problem to the plan to the payoff.
Introduction: the present situation and the need.
Objectives: what the project aims to achieve.
Method: who does what, when and how.
Benefits: what changes for the better.

narration.en: Let us draw a proposal, section by section on the board, one box at a time.

prompt.en: Arrange the sections of a proposal for a school herb garden.

narration.en: Arrange the sections of a proposal for a school herb garden.

steps.en: Title: A Herb Garden for Our School
Introduction: an unused plot behind the science block and students with little contact with plants
Objectives: to grow medicinal herbs and teach practical botany
Plan of action: Eco Club volunteers prepare beds in July and plant in August
Resources: seeds, tools and a water connection, about ₹8,000
Benefits: hands-on learning, a greener campus and herbs for the canteen
Conclusion: approval is requested to begin in July

explanation.en: A proposal moves from the need to the aims, the plan, the cost, the benefits and the request.

body.en: Use all the information given in the question and expand each note into a clear point. Keep sections short and to the point; headings help the reader find information fast. Be specific: dates, numbers, people responsible. Prefer the impersonal and passive (It is proposed that a committee be formed …; The garden will be maintained by …). Avoid emotional appeals and exaggeration: a proposal persuades by being practical and complete.

prompt.en: Sort each sentence into the section of the proposal where it belongs.

narration.en: Sort each sentence into the section of the proposal where it belongs.

text.en: At present, food waste from the canteen is thrown out with other garbage.
To reduce the waste sent to landfill by half.
Two compost pits will be dug behind the canteen in June.
Class representatives will collect waste every afternoon.
The compost will feed the school garden and save money on fertiliser.
To teach students how waste can become a resource.

explanation.en: The introduction describes the situation; objectives start "To…"; the plan says who does what and when; benefits describe the good results.

problem.en: Expand these notes into the "Plan of action" of a proposal: reading corner – library – 2 shelves, cushions – student volunteers – Saturday book swap – start next term.

steps.en: It is proposed that a reading corner be set up in the school library at the start of next term.
Two shelves and floor cushions will be arranged near the windows.
A team of student volunteers will manage the corner and keep a simple register.
A book swap will be held every Saturday, where students may exchange books they have read.

answer.en: A clear, impersonal plan of action with who, what, where and when.

body.en: Every proposal answers three questions: what is wrong now (problem), what we will do (plan), and what will get better (payoff). If a section does not serve one of these, cut it.
